questions.question_html: The following information was provided by PQR Ltd. for the year ended 31st March, 2024: (1) Gross Profit Ratio was 25% for the year, which amounts to ₹3,75,000. (2) Company sold goods for cash only. (3) Opening inventory was lesser than closing inventory by ₹25,000. (4) Wages paid during the year ₹5,55,000. (5) Office expenses paid during the year ₹35,000. (6) Selling expenses paid during the year ₹15,000. (7) Dividend paid during the year ₹40,000. (8) Bank Loan repaid during the year ₹2,05,000 (included interest ₹5,000). (9) Trade Payables on 31st March, 2023 were ₹50,000 and on 31st March, 2024 were ₹35,000. (10) Amount paid to Trade payables during the year ₹6,10,000. (11) Income Tax paid during the year amounts to ₹55,000 (Provision for taxation as on 31st March, 2024 ₹30,000). (12) Investments of ₹8,20,000 sold during the year at a profit of ₹20,000. (13) Depreciation on furniture amounts to ₹40,000. (14) Depreciation on other PPE amounts to ₹20,000. (15) Plant and Machinery purchased on 15th November, 2023 for ₹3,50,000. (16) On 31st March, 2024 ₹2,00,000, 7% Debentures were issued at face value in an exchange for a plant. (17) Cash and Cash equivalents on 31st March, 2023 ₹2,25,000. Required: (i) Prepare cash flow statement for the year ended 31st March, 2024, using direct method. (ii) Calculate cash flow from operating activities, using indirect method.
questions.answer_html:
(i) PQR Ltd. – Cash Flow Statement for the year ended 31st March, 2024 (direct method)

Cash sales (₹3,75,000/25%)15,00,000
Less: Cash payments for trade payables(6,10,000)
Less: Wages Paid(5,55,000)
Less: Office and selling expenses (35,000+15,000)(50,000)
Cash generated from operations before taxes2,85,000
Income tax paid(55,000)
Net cash generated from operating activities (A)2,30,000
Sale of investments (8,20,000+20,000)8,40,000
Payments for purchase of Plant & machinery(3,50,000)
Net cash used in investing activities (B)4,90,000
Bank loan repayment (including interest)(2,05,000)
Dividend paid(40,000)
Net cash used in financing activities (C)(2,45,000)
Net increase in cash (A+B+C)4,75,000
Cash and cash equivalents at beginning of the period2,25,000
Cash and cash equivalents at end of the period7,00,000

(ii) Cash Flow from Operating Activities – indirect method

Net Profit for the year before tax and extraordinary items2,80,000
Add: Depreciation60,000
Add: Interest Paid5,000
Less: Profit on Sale of Investments(20,000)
Net Profit after Adjustment for Non-Cash Items3,25,000
Less: Decrease in trade payables15,000
Less: Increase in inventory25,000
Cash generated from operations before taxes2,85,000

Working note – net profit before tax: Gross profit 3,75,000 − (Office/selling expenses 50,000 + Depreciation 60,000 + Interest paid 5,000 = 1,15,000) = 2,60,000; add profit on sale of investments 20,000 = 2,80,000.
questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating the ₹2,05,000 bank loan repayment as entirely a financing outflow without separating the ₹5,000 interest component, or forgetting that the debenture-for-plant exchange (a non-cash transaction) must be excluded entirely from the cash flow statement.

questions.question_html:
Following information was extracted from the books of A Ltd. for the year ended 31st March, 2025:

  1. Net profit before taking into account income tax and after taking into account the following items was ₹60 lakhs: (a) Depreciation on Property, Plant & Equipment ₹14,00,000. (b) Discount on issue of debentures written off ₹90,000. (c) Interest on debentures paid ₹8,70,000. (d) Investment of Book value ₹7,00,000 sold for ₹7,50,000. (e) Interest received on Investments ₹1,40,000.
  2. Income tax paid during the year ₹25,60,000.
  3. Company issued 1,20,000 Equity Shares of ₹10 each at a premium of 20% on 10th April, 2024.
  4. 40,000, 9% Preference Shares of ₹100 each were redeemed on 31st March, 2025 at a premium of 5%.
  5. Dividend paid during the year amounted to ₹22 Lakhs (Incl. dividend distribution tax).
  6. A new Plant costing ₹14 Lakhs was purchased in part exchange of an old plant on 1st January, 2025. The book value of the old plant was ₹16 Lakhs but the vendor took over the old plant at a value of ₹12 Lakhs only. The balance amount was paid to vendor through cheque on 30th March, 2025.
  7. Company decided to value inventory at cost, whereas previously the practice was to value inventory at cost less 10%. The inventory according to books on 31.03.2025 was ₹29,52,000 (cost less 10%). The inventory on 31.03.2024 was correctly valued at ₹27,00,000.
  8. Current Assets and Current Liabilities in the beginning and at the end of year 2024-2025 were as: Inventory ₹27,00,000 (01.4.2024) / ₹29,52,000 (31.3.2025); Trade Receivables ₹6,54,000 / ₹6,26,400; Cash & Bank Balances ₹4,81,400 / ₹7,41,000; Trade Payables ₹5,69,400 / ₹5,74,600; Outstanding Expenses ₹1,94,000 / ₹2,02,800.

You are required to prepare a Cash Flow Statement for the operating & investing activity year ended 31st March, 2025 as per AS 3 (revised) using the indirect method.

questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating the change in inventory valuation policy (cost-less-10% to cost) as an ordinary working-capital movement rather than first restating the closing figure to a comparable cost basis, and separately, showing the full ₹14,00,000 cost of the new Plant as a cash outflow instead of only the ₹2,00,000 actually paid by cheque (the ₹12,00,000 part-exchange being a non-cash transaction).

questions.topic_text: Topic 2.6: Fixed asset acquisitions and disposals reported gross, not netted, in the cash flow statement

topics.topic_name: Calculation of Cash Flows from Financing Activities

questions.why: Rank 12 topic (Calculation of Cash Flows from Financing Activities); RTP September 2025.
questions.question_html: Garden Ltd. acquired plant and machinery for ₹20 lakhs and sold furniture and fixtures for ₹5 lakhs in the same year. Can the company disclose net cash outflow towards purchase of fixed assets in the cash flow statement per AS 3?
questions.answer_html: No. Per AS 3 para 21, major classes of gross cash receipts and gross cash payments from investing and financing activities must be reported separately, except for the specific items permitted to be reported net under paras 22 and 24 — acquisition and disposal of fixed assets is not among those permitted items. The company cannot net the ₹20 lakh purchase against the ₹5 lakh disposal; both must be shown as separate gross cash flow lines.
questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees assumed netting was acceptable since both items relate to fixed assets, not checking the specific, limited list of items AS 3 actually permits to be reported net.

questions.topic_text: Topic 2.3: Classification of cash flows across operating, investing and financing activities for loans/advances, investment/dividend and insurance-claim items
questions.why: Rank 91 topic (Classification of Cash Flow Activities); 77% match to an ICAI Study Material question; RTP September 2024.
questions.question_html:
Purse Ltd., a non financial company has the following entries in its Bank Account. It has sought your advice on the treatment of the same for preparing Cash Flow Statement.

  1. Loans and Advances given to the following and interest earned on them:
    1. to suppliers
    2. to employees
    3. to its subsidiaries companies
  2. Investment made in subsidiary Wallet Ltd. and dividend received
  3. Dividend paid for the year
  4. Insurance claim received against loss of property, plant and equipment by fire.

Discuss in the context of AS 3 ‘Cash Flow Statement’.
questions.answer_html:
ItemClassification
(i)(1) Loans/advances and interest — to suppliersCash flows from operating activities
(i)(2) Loans/advances and interest — to employeesCash flows from operating activities
(i)(3) Loans/advances and interest — to its subsidiary companiesCash flows from investing activities
(ii) Investment made in subsidiary company and dividend receivedCash flows from investing activities
(iii) Dividend paid for the yearCash flows from financing activities
(iv) Insurance claim received against loss of property, plant and equipment by fire(no classification stated — see extraction note)
questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is classifying loans/advances to subsidiaries the same way as loans to suppliers or employees (operating activity), without recognising that an inter-company loan of this kind is an investing activity from the lending company's perspective.

questions.topic_text: Topic 2.3: Classification of cash flow activities - operating, investing, financing, and cash equivalents
questions.why: Rank 91 topic (Classification of Cash Flow Activities); RTP January 2025.
questions.question_html:
Classify the following activities as (1) Operating Activities, (2) Investing Activities, (3) Financing Activities (4) Cash Equivalents.

  1. Proceeds from long-term borrowings.
  2. Proceeds from Trade receivables.
  3. Trading Commission received.
  4. Redemption of Preference Shares.
  5. Proceeds from sale of investment
  6. Interim Dividend paid on equity shares.
  7. Interest received on debentures held as investment.
  8. Dividend received on shares held as investments.
  9. Rent received on property held as investment.
  10. Dividend paid on Preference shares.
  11. Marketable Securities
questions.answer_html:
Operating Activities: b, c.

Investing Activities: e, g, h, i.

Financing Activities: a, d, f, j.

Cash Equivalents: k
questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is classifying interest and dividend received on investments as operating activities because they arise from routine treasury income, missing that AS 3 classifies these as investing activities from the recipient's perspective, reserving operating classification for the enterprise's principal revenue-generating activities.
